# QML describes the view {#sec-qml}

QML works best when it describes what the view should show. Bind a property to state, send a
user action to C++, and let the binding update the view later.

## Bindings keep state connected {#sec-bindings}

A binding is a live relationship, not an assignment. Sketchbook disables Undo from C++ state
and sends the action back to the store.

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/CanvasPage.qml"}

```qml
                ToolButton {\n                    icon.source: Theme.icon("undo-2")
                    onClicked: root.store.undo()\n                }
```

:::

Do not overwrite a bound property in JavaScript. Change the source that owns the value.
An assignment such as `button.enabled = true` replaces the binding on `enabled`; it does not
temporarily override it. Later changes to `canUndo` would no longer update that button.

## Components have typed inputs {#sec-components}

A reusable component declares what it needs with `required property` and emits its own
signals. This makes missing wiring a load-time error instead of a surprising runtime state.

For example, `CanvasPage` defines a `Swatch` with a required color and a `picked` signal. The
parent decides what a picked color means; the swatch only handles its own presentation and input.

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/CanvasPage.qml"}

```qml
    component Swatch: AbstractButton {
            border.color: swatch.checked ? Theme.accent : Theme.border\n        }\n    }
```

:::

Typed properties and function parameters let QML tooling check the contract. Qualify access
to a component's properties through its `id`, so a reader and the tools can see which object
owns the value. Keep declarations, signals, functions, object properties, and children in a
consistent order.

## Lists use models {#sec-lists}

A model reports precise insert, update, and removal changes. The view keeps its scroll
position and delegates instead of rebuilding everything.

The sketchbook model exposes roles such as `name` and `strokeCount`. A delegate declares the
roles it needs as required properties. This adapted example keeps the list and its delegate,
but leaves out the extra row controls in the real
[SketchbookPage.qml](https://github.com/deeedob/qt-kickstart/blob/main/src/sketchbook/SketchbookPage.qml):

```qml
ListView {
    model: root.viewModel.model

    delegate: ItemDelegate {
        required property string name
        required property int strokeCount

        text: name
    }
}
```

When a sketch is added, the C++ model announces the insertion before and after changing its
data. The view can then create just the new delegate:

::: {.snippet source="src/sketchbook/SketchListModel.cpp"}

```cpp
void SketchListModel::prepend
    endInsertRows();\n}
```

:::

## Layout follows intent {#sec-positioning}

Use anchors for a relationship to an edge, layouts for a row or column, and positioners for
simple repeated content. Keep logic small. If a QML function starts making decisions about
application state, move that decision to C++.

Anchors express relationships such as filling a parent. Layouts share available space and
respect implicit, minimum, and preferred sizes. Positioners arrange children without the full
layout negotiation. Choose the smallest mechanism that expresses the intended relationship,
and avoid assigning geometry that a layout already controls.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/canvas/CanvasPage.qml` and `src/sketchbook/SketchListModel.cpp`

**Read more:** [QML coding conventions](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qml-codingconventions.html).
:::
